judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: The element is an empty anchor, , at the top of main. It has no href and no content. claimTrue: yes. The CDP data in the snapshot gives it role link, focusable, with no name, so Chrome does expose it as a nameless link. captureDiffers: no. The live HTML fetched on 2026-11-21 has the identical element. elementFails: I lean yes. tabindex=0 puts an invisible element in the tab order, and Chrome announces it as a "link" with no name or purpose. But a concrete counter-reading holds up. HTML-AAM maps an a element without href to generic, and the ACT rule for link names (and axe's link-name) does not apply to it. The element is a skip-link-style target, not a control users perceive. Many auditors would report this as a meaningless tab stop (2.4.3, and 2.4.7 since it is invisible) or as a best-practice issue, not as a 4.1.2 user-interface component without a name. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree, so the label is uncertain.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the language-switcher link "繁體中文" (href /zhT-CN/Recalls) on a page with lang="en". Neither the link nor its li carries a lang attribute. claimTrue: yes. The snapshot shows no lang on the link or its ancestors below html, so the link inherits en. elementFails: yes. The text is Traditional Chinese, not a proper name, technical term or English vernacular. An English voice cannot pronounce it, and nothing identifies its language. Understanding 3.1.2's "Alternative language links" example is exactly this pattern (each language name, written in that language, marked with lang), and H58 is the sufficient technique. Skeptic checks: the live HTML fetched on 2026-11-21 has the same bare <a> inside <li id="zh-hant">, and the snapshot is post-script, so no script adds lang. captureDiffers: no. The claim names the failure and the right fix.

judgments.label: true_positive

It inherits en in the snapshot. elementFails: yes. "Español" is a Spanish word, not part of English vernacular, so it falls outside 3.1.2's exceptions. Understanding 3.1.2's "Alternative language links" example treats language names written in their own language (Deutsch, Français) as phrases that need lang. That rules out the proper-name exception and the "single word belongs to the surrounding language" readings I considered. captureDiffers: no.
